rubrics.criterion: The response contrasts Euclidean geometry in high school math competitions (AMC, AIME, Olympiads) with that in standard American high school curricula.
The response is written for an audience familiar with standard high school geometry but without competitive math experience.
The response includes at least one clear example of a problem-solving technique common in math competitions but not typically taught in standard high school classes.
The response includes at least one clear example of a theorem used in math competitions but not typically covered in standard high school geometry courses.
The response distinguishes the depth, rigor, or proof expectations in competition geometry versus standard curriculum.
The response explains how competition problems often require multi-step insight or non-routine application, unlike typical textbook exercises.
The response identifies specific theorems (e.g., Ceva’s Theorem, Menelaus’s Theorem, Power of a Point, Angle Bisector Theorem extensions) used in competitions but omitted from standard curricula.
The response illustrates how auxiliary constructions (e.g., adding circles, parallel lines, or incenters) are frequently required in competition problems but rarely emphasized in standard classes.
The response highlights the role of synthetic geometry reasoning in competitions, as opposed to the more formulaic or computational approach in standard classes.
The response compares the problem structures: competition problems often lack explicit solution pathways, unlike scaffolded textbook problems.
The response addresses the expectation of elegant or insight-based solutions in competitions versus procedural mastery in standard classes.
The response notes the limited time pressure and strategic thinking in competitions (e.g., AMC multiple choice with tricks), contrasting with homework-style pacing in school.
The response references actual named competitions (AMC, AIME, Olympiads) as specified in the prompt.
The response avoids assuming prior knowledge of competition math beyond standard high school geometry.
The response uses accessible language and avoids unexplained jargon from advanced geometry or olympiad training.
The response clearly explains any technical term (e.g., cyclic quadrilateral, homothety) before or when used.
The response includes a concrete competition-style problem example with solution steps demonstrating non-standard techniques.
The response contrasts the pedagogical goals: conceptual depth and creativity in competitions vs. foundational fluency in standard classes.
The response acknowledges that some advanced topics (e.g., coordinate bashing, trigonometric Ceva) are used in competitions but absent from standard curricula.
The response does not misrepresent standard high school geometry as entirely lacking proofs or rigor.
The response does not claim that competition geometry replaces or is formally part of the standard curriculum.
The response avoids asserting that standard geometry teaching is ineffective or universally shallow.
The response does not fabricate or misattribute theorems (e.g., attributing Ceva’s Theorem to a different mathematician).
The response does not present competition techniques as trivial or obvious to standard curriculum students, preserving appropriate challenge level.
The response maintains a blog-style tone appropriate for informal but informative exposition.
The response integrates examples naturally within the narrative rather than presenting them as isolated technical appendices.
The response does not omit the fact that some competition techniques can be derived from standard knowledge, even if not taught directly.
The response distinguishes between curriculum content and classroom practice, avoiding conflation of the two.
